newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Prodi sees agreement on welfare reform.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Prodi sees agreement on welfare reform.

text.p: Prime Minister Romani Prodi was quoted on Sunday as saying he was confident that the hard-left Communist Refoundation party would eventually support welfare reform.

Prodi's centre-left coalition government almost fell in April when Communist Refoundation, which gives his coalition a majority in the lower house of parliament, refused to support the deployment of a security force to Albania.
Refoundation have threatened to rebel again over government plans to curb social spending and shake up Italy's pension system in preparation for the launch of a single European currency in 1999.
But in an interview with Milan newspaper Corriere della Sera, Prodi said he was confident Refoundation eventually would support welfare reform.

"This time I don't think we'll see games from the left to climb over us," Corriere quoted him as saying. "We've been working for months to avoid that. We have made clear what's at stake, the roles, the responsibilities...
"The situation today is different from before. We have let questions over welfare mature with a long debate.
"It's not an explosive affair like the Albanian crisis. We've given everyone time to get to grips with the problems. I have the impression there's a broad willingness to reach an agreement."
Talks between the government, union leaders and employers on how to reform the welfare state began on June 18 but ran into immediate difficulties over pensions.
Prodi called for a review of the country's generous early retirement system which allows Italians to draw a pension based on length of service rather than age.
He also said future pension spending should be pegged to growth in Gross Domestic Product.
Refoundation has insisted there should be no cuts in social and pension spending while the trades union federation has accused the government of ignoring employment issues.
The government has said it wants to reach an agreement with all sides by the end of September, and Prodi ruled out ditching some of the proposals to ensure others were accepted.

"I'm aiming at the whole target," he said. "The entire agreement, complete in every part, before the end of September. We're moving forward at a brisk pace and the various parties are working in parallel."
